title: Harun al-Rashid's Sons Go to War
text:
Harun al-Rashid, the most famous caliph of the Abbasid dynasty, had two sons born months apart, in 786 and 787. Abdallah, later called al-Mamun, was the elder, but his mother was a Persian slave concubine. Muhammad, later called al-Amin, was the son of Zubayda, Harun's wife and herself a granddaughter of a caliph.

Harun tried to settle the succession in advance. In 802, on pilgrimage to Mecca, he made both sons swear to an agreement. Al-Amin would be caliph in Baghdad, while al-Mamun would govern the vast eastern province of Khurasan and succeed his brother. The documents were hung inside the Kaaba itself, to make them sacred.

Harun died in 809. Within a year al-Amin, urged on by his advisers, moved to break the agreement, removing his brother from the succession in favor of his own young son. Al-Mamun, supported by Khurasan, refused. In 811 war broke out. Al-Mamun's general Tahir ibn Husayn defeated the caliph's much larger army and advanced on Baghdad. The great city was besieged for more than a year, and whole quarters were destroyed. In September 813 al-Amin was captured while trying to escape and was killed.

Al-Mamun became caliph and later presided over a golden age of learning. The historian al-Tabari recorded the war in detail.
lesson: A parent can divide an inheritance on paper, but only goodwill between children keeps the peace. Agreements that leave rivals equally powerful invite conflict.
people: Harun al-Rashid, al-Amin, al-Mamun, Zubayda, Tahir ibn Husayn
source: Al-Tabari, History of the Prophets and Kings, vols. 30 to 31 (English trans. SUNY)
